system: You are a meticulous senior equity research editor. You audit news summaries written for analysts. You are strict about factual accuracy and you do not reward length.
prompt:
An analyst covering JPMorgan Chase (JPM) will read the SUMMARY instead of the ARTICLE.
Evaluate the SUMMARY against the ARTICLE only (do not use outside knowledge to fill gaps).

<article>
HEADLINE: Update: JPMorgan Asset Management Seeks to Convert Certain Municipal Funds Into ETFs

BODY:
03:36 PM EST, 12/09/2025 (MT Newswires) -- (Updates with the company's statement throughout.)

JPMorgan Chase's (JPM) investment management division JPMorgan Asset Management said Tuesday it plans to convert certain US mutual funds into exchange-traded funds in 2026.

The proposed conversions, if approved by the board of the funds in February, are expected to provide benefits like flexibility, increased transparency and enhanced tax efficiency, JPMorgan Asset Management said.

JPMorgan believes that these funds, including JPMorgan New York Tax Free Bond Fund, JPMorgan California Tax Free Bond Fund, JPMorgan Preferred and Income Securities Fund, and JPMorgan US GARP Equity Fund are "well suited" for the ETF structure, the investment management arm said, adding that the combined assets of the funds are about $4.6 billion.

Price: 302.16, Change: -13.05, Percent Change: -4.14
</article>

<summary>
JPMorgan Asset Management announced plans to convert several US mutual funds—including the JPMorgan New York Tax Free Bond Fund, California Tax Free Bond Fund, Preferred and Income Securities Fund, and US GARP Equity Fund—into ETFs in 2026, pending board approval in February. The funds, representing roughly $4.6 billion in combined assets, are seen as well-suited for the ETF structure, offering benefits such as greater flexibility, transparency, and tax efficiency. This move reflects JPMorgan's continued push to expand its ETF lineup amid broader industry trends favoring ETF conversions. JPM shares fell 4.14% to $302.16 on the day of the announcement. JPMorgan Chase also announced a new $5 billion share buyback program.
</summary>

Step 1 - Claim check. List every claim in the summary that is NOT supported by the article: invented facts,
wrong numbers, wrong direction (e.g. "rose" vs "fell"), wrong company, unattributed rumours stated as fact,
or speculative links to JPM that the article does not make.
Step 2 - Omissions. List the most important investment-relevant facts about JPM in the article that
the summary misses (at most 3).
Step 3 - Score each criterion from 1 to 5:

faithfulness
  5 every claim supported | 4 minor imprecision with no investment impact | 3 one unsupported or distorted claim
  2 several unsupported claims, or one material error (number, direction, company) | 1 largely unsupported
ticker_focus  (does it tell a JPM analyst what matters, and represent how central JPM really is?)
  5 centred on what matters for JPM, and says so plainly if JPM is peripheral or absent
  3 a generic article summary; the JPM angle is implicit or buried
  1 ignores JPM, or implies the article is about / important for JPM when it is not
coverage  (key investment-relevant facts: the event, key figures, attribution)
  5 all key facts | 3 misses some important facts | 1 misses the main point
conciseness
  5 no filler, easy to scan | 3 some redundancy or filler | 1 verbose or hard to parse

Return only JSON:
{
  "unsupported_claims": ["..."],
  "missing_key_facts": ["..."],
  "overstates_ticker_link": true | false,
  "faithfulness": 1-5,
  "ticker_focus": 1-5,
  "coverage": 1-5,
  "conciseness": 1-5
}
